title: The teacher
hookLine: in Tibetan practice the teacher is central; students are told to check a teacher for years first

cards: A contractor gets his references checked. A dentist gets her reviews read. Yet people sometimes hand their whole inner life, their time, their money, their trust, to a charismatic stranger after one inspiring weekend.
Tibetan Buddhism puts the teacher at the center of the path. And the same tradition tells students, in writing: slow down. Check first.
Some texts say to take years.

teach.b: Lama is the Tibetan word for the Sanskrit guru. Guru literally means heavy: someone of weight, whose words land. Tibetans give lama their own warm explanations too; a common one says it means none higher.
Why is the teacher so central here?
Because many Vajrayana practices pass from person to person.

A teacher reads the text aloud so the student receives it, gives permission for a practice, and shows how it's done, the way a music teacher shows you how to hold the bow. You can read about the violin forever.
At some point, someone has to hear you play. But the same tradition insists on caution.
A text called the Fifty Verses on the Guru tells teacher and student to examine each other first, and Tibetan teachers often say this can take as long as twelve years.
The Dalai Lama has said many times that students should scrutinize a teacher carefully, and that no one should follow an instruction that goes against the teaching or against basic ethics.

teach.h: SIGNS OF A GOOD TEACHER, AND WARNINGS.
teach.b: Classic lists describe a good teacher as disciplined, calm, learned, loving, and tireless in teaching.
And there are warning signs anyone can see: pressure, secrecy, money that's never explained, being cut off from friends, behavior that breaks the very precepts being taught.

Recent decades have shown why this matters: some communities have been hurt by teachers who abused their trust, and Tibetan teachers, the Dalai Lama among them, have said such harm should be made public.
The heart of it is simple. Trust is given slowly, and it stays open to question.

how: In Tibetan Buddhism students usually study with a lama who gives teachings, reading transmissions and empowerments; many teachers advise students to observe a teacher for a long time before committing to one.

games.q: match what the tradition says about teachers.

s: Tibetan tradition tells students to trust a teacher at once
it tells teacher and student to examine each other, sometimes for years.
the Dalai Lama has said students should scrutinize a teacher
and not follow an instruction that goes against the teaching or basic ethics.
many Vajrayana practices are passed from person to person
a teacher reads the text aloud, gives permission and shows how it's done.

games.q: you've found an inspiring teacher. after a month, they ask you to keep the group's finances secret and to stop seeing old friends. what does the tradition itself advise?
o: slow down, keep checking, and step back if it breaks ethics.
games.why: the tradition that makes the teacher central also says to examine a teacher carefully and not follow instructions against basic ethics.

practice: Think of someone who taught you something that mattered, a coach, a grandparent, a boss, a teacher in any field, and silently name two or three things that made them trustworthy: maybe they admitted mistakes, or never asked for more than they gave.
Then let the list go and sit with the breath, knowing that you, too, get to be careful about whom you trust.
